mechanism.description: Higher GCS indicates preserved level of consciousness and typically correlates with smaller infarct volume and lower baseline stroke severity — such patients have more salvageable penumbra and therefore greater absolute benefit from timely reperfusion. Patients with better consciousness at baseline generally have lower rates of early complications (including aspiration and early intracranial complications) and better capacity to recover function after reperfusion, increasing the chance that reperfusion translates into independent functional outcome. Severely depressed consciousness often reflects large infarcts, brainstem involvement, or early malignant edema where thrombolysis may be less able to reverse disabling injury and may carry proportionally higher risks (e.g., symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage), attenuating net benefit. Clinical registries and pooled analyses of thrombolysis trials have shown that baseline neurological status modifies absolute outcomes after reperfusion therapies; therefore GCS — a simple bedside measure — is plausibly an effect modifier of alteplase benefit. GCS is routinely available at presentation and largely independent of some imaging markers, allowing practical subgrouping for clinical decision support if validated.

Severely reduced consciousness (GCS <= 8) generally reflects large ischemic burden, brainstem involvement, or malignant cerebral oedema — situations with reduced salvageable penumbra where reperfusion is less likely to produce functional recovery. Extensive early infarction and blood–brain barrier disruption associated with coma increases risk of hemorrhagic transformation after thrombolysis; several registry and clinical reports show higher symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH) and mortality among comatose/low-GCS stroke patients receiving reperfusion therapies. Low GCS identifies a population with very high baseline risk of poor outcome regardless of treatment; relative benefit of thrombolysis may therefore be small in absolute terms and the absolute increase in bleeding risk may outweigh any modest chance of neurological improvement. Clinical practice and trial exclusions often omit profoundly comatose patients from aggressive reperfusion because predicted benefit is low and risk of complications high — consistent with a priori expectation of limited or harmful treatment effect in this subgroup.

Ceiling effect on absolute risk reduction: patients with minimal neurologic impairment at baseline already have high absolute probability of independence at 6 months, so the same relative treatment effect translates into a smaller absolute risk difference and larger number-needed-to-treat. Risk–benefit trade-off: the absolute benefit in a low-risk subgroup may be offset by the absolute risk of treatment-related harms (symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage), making net clinical benefit smaller or negligible in GCS==15 patients. Empirical precedent: prior stroke trial subgroup analyses and observational studies frequently find smaller absolute benefits from thrombolysis among patients with minor stroke or low baseline severity (despite similar relative effects), supporting the plausibility of effect modification on the absolute scale. Measurement/construct plausibility: GCS primarily measures consciousness level; a GCS of 15 identifies patients without depressed consciousness who often have less extensive ischemia, faster spontaneous recovery, and lower baseline prognostic uncertainty—factors that reduce marginal gains from reperfusion. Clinical decision-making context: equipoise exists for very mild strokes — many guidelines and trials highlight uncertain net benefit in mild deficits, consistent with the hypothesis that fully alert patients receive limited absolute benefit.

Pathophysiology: Acute hyperglycaemia during cerebral ischemia increases anaerobic glycolysis and lactic acid production in ischemic tissue, promoting infarct growth and reducing salvageable penumbra — mechanisms that plausibly reduce the net benefit of reperfusion therapies. Haemorrhagic transformation risk: Hyperglycaemia exacerbates blood–brain barrier disruption and oxidative stress in reperfused tissue in preclinical models, increasing risk of haemorrhagic transformation after reperfusion and thereby potentially blunting functional gains from thrombolysis. Observational clinical evidence: Multiple observational cohorts report associations between higher admission glucose and larger infarct volumes, increased symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage (sICH) after thrombolysis, and worse 3–6 month functional outcomes, consistent with an interaction where hyperglycaemia worsens outcome even after reperfusion. Therapeutic implication and guideline relevance: Because hyperglycaemia is modifiable acutely and some clinical guidance recommends correction, it is clinically relevant to know whether marked hyperglycaemia modifies the randomized alteplase effect size (i.e., whether benefit is reduced enough to affect treatment decisions). Distinguishing acute stress from chronic glycaemic state: Acute admission glucose may reflect stress hyperglycaemia (poor prognostic sign) or poorly controlled diabetes; both biological pathways plausibly interact with reperfusion but may differ in magnitude — so investigation should adjust for diabetes history or HbA1c when available.

Salvageable tissue and reperfusion biology: Timely thrombolysis can restore perfusion and salvage penumbral tissue. Modest hyperglycaemia may not significantly increase lactic acidosis, blood–brain barrier disruption, or oxidative stress to the degree that it neutralizes thrombolysis benefit seen in more severe hyperglycaemia. Heterogeneous observational findings: Several cohort studies and secondary analyses of thrombolysis cohorts report that mild-to-moderate hyperglycaemia is not uniformly associated with reduced recanalization rates or absence of functional benefit after thrombolysis, suggesting preserved or only slightly attenuated treatment effect in this range. mechanism.description: Pharmacologic dosing rule: Alteplase is dosed at 0.9 mg/kg with an absolute maximum total dose (commonly 90 mg). Patients weighing >=100 kg exceed the weight at which the 0.9 mg/kg rule reaches the cap (0.9*100 = 90 mg), so heavier patients will typically receive less than 0.9 mg/kg, leading to lower systemic mg/kg exposure. Biologic plausibility: Lower per-kilogram exposure of tPA may reduce clot lysis probability and vessel recanalization rates, which are mechanistically linked to improved functional outcomes after ischemic stroke. Thus dose under-exposure in very heavy patients plausibly decreases treatment efficacy. Obesity-related pathophysiology and comorbidity: Very high body weight is associated with pro-thrombotic states, endothelial dysfunction, and higher prevalence of comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension, OSA) that may both increase stroke severity and blunt recovery; these factors could interact with reduced drug exposure to yield lower net benefit. Empirical signals from prior analyses: Although direct randomized evidence is limited, observational and subgroup reports have suggested altered outcomes or different safety/efficacy profiles in very heavy patients receiving weight-capped medications; this supports testing for treatment-by-weight interaction in IST-3 data. Operational importance: If a true interaction exists, it has direct clinical implications (consider alternative dosing strategies, individualized dosing, or weight-specific counseling), making it a relevant hypothesis despite anticipated small subgroup sizes.
